subtopic: REPORT ON MEETINGS RESPECTING INTERNATIONAL MONETARY CRISIS

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: REPORT ON MEETINGS RESPECTING INTERNATIONAL MONETARY CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to give a brief report on the important meetings in Bonn last week of the ministers and central bank governors of the Group of Ten. The meetings were called to discuss the measures that could be taken to restore equilibrium in the international monetary system which had been disturbed by massive speculative capital movements involving some European currencies. The governor of the Bank of Canada and I participated in the discussions.
The authorities of the Federal Republic of Germany announced their decision to take parliamentary action immediately to alter their border tax adjustments in such a way as to reduce substantially the German trade surplus. They are also taking steps to inhibit the inflow of short term capital.
The French authorities have announced that they will take steps immediately to reduce their budgetary deficit, to restrict the use of credit, to slow down price and wage increases, and to impose foreign exchange controls. '
No change in the par values of the Deutschmark or the French franc is involved in any of these measures.
A new central bank credit facility for France was arranged in the amount of two billion U.S. dollars. The Bank of Canada's share of this facility is 100 million U.S. dollars. The new facility is in addition to France's substantial drawing facilities in the International Monetary Fund.
The authorities' of the countries concerned are determined to seek a better equilibrium in their international payments, to counter speculation, and to offset the effect on exchange reserves of destabilizing short term capital flows. The measures taken are an expression of this determination. The response of financial markets in Europe and North America today has been encouraging. Throughout the period of disturbance the Canadian dollar has remained strong.
Mr. Speaker, if the house will permit I will table the communique issued at the end of the meetings of the Group of Ten.

speechtext:
It is difficult for me to believe that the Minister of Finance had not consulted the government of Canada about commitments that would be appropriate on behalf of Canada at this time. I had also hoped to receive some information from the minister's statement. Without being offensive, let me say he has not told us anything we had not read in the press.
The impression one gets is that the decision of the government of France not to de-
November 25, 1968

International Monetary Crisis value the franc took everybody completely by surprise. The minister has not indicated whether this is so, but this is the impression we have gained from the news media, and it has not been corrected by the minister. In addition, this decision has placed a severe strain upon some other international currencies, notably the pound sterling; and the minister has not made any comment in this regard nor about the measures the British government has had to support within the last few days, constituting another series of tough measures.
Frankly, I must say it does not seem to me the minister has given us any information or any reassurance in respect of the existing situation, and in view of experience during the past year I am sure we all agree that if these difficulties spread they could spread to us as well. After all, this is the third monetary crisis this year. As recently as October 7 the Minister of Finance returned from a series of international finance meetings in South America, rather blandly I thought- satisfied and optimistic about arrangements that had been made to "enhance", as he put it, "the stability of sterling and of the international monetary situation".
At that time I could not share the minister's satisfaction, and I was disappointed that more progress had not been made in the area of strengthening international currency arrangements. I said then that the proper time had arrived for more permanent arrangements to be made, and that progress had been slow. What seemed to be appropriate a month ago has become a matter of extreme urgency today. I suggest to the Minister of Finance in Canada that he ought to take the lead in pressing with utmost vigour the necessity for a new international currencies arrangement.
I believe the minister is living in a paradise of some sort if he thinks the measures taken to get us out of recent crises can be regarded as satisfactory over the long term without more permanent arrangements, or if he thinks for a moment that the dollar, and therefore the Canadian economy, can escape the possible ramifications of this crisis.
Let me repeat the need for immediate further action for more permanent arrangements, recognizing the instability of the present situation and the efforts to, in fact, stabilize the international monetary situation.

subtopic: REPORT ON MEETINGS RESPECTING INTERNATIONAL MONETARY CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister would be the first to agree that his report told us nothing we have


not already read in the newspapers, and that the hope expressed in the report is entirely ill-founded; that the situation has not improved, that the crisis has not ended and that the foundation has been laid for further crises, particularly in respect of the British pound and probably the French franc and the German mark.
As the Leader of the Opposition has said, we have experienced three serious international monetary crises in the last year in respect of the British pound, the United States dollar and the French franc. None of the steps taken or being taken have solved or gone any distance toward solving this international problem.
I want us to note that the results of these discussions have been not only austerity measures in France but serious austerity measures in Britain. I do not say that the Canadian government is responsible or that the Minister of Finance alone could do anything to solve this problem, but as one citizen of the world I am fed up to the teeth by the fact that the entire world can be set on its ear partly by the unscrupulous gambling of speculators and partly because of other reasons which I realize are there.
It is time the international community took steps to stop this speculation on the international monetary markets even if it should mean closing the various markets on which currencies can be bought and sold, except for the legitimate purposes of trading and tourist travelling. I suggest it is time that a country like Canada took that kind of initiative at the International Monetary Fund, at the World Bank and at all these international meetings of ministers of finance. It is just shameful that this dark and dusty corner of international monetary gambling should be able to trap the world and its policies.
Second, I suggest it is time we in this country in particular took the initiative and started discussions to end the pegged rates of the various currencies. The other day when the hon. member for Regina East (Mr. Burton) asked the Prime Minister whether the government would not consider a floating exchange rate, the Prime Minister's irritating way of answering it, as with some other questions, was simply "Heavens, no." That may be a nice undergraduate answer, but it certainly does not deal with a very serious problem.
The fact is that this pegging of the various currency rates across the world is the equivalent of the gold standard in principle. We
November 25. 1968

have been in exactly the same position in the last ten years as we were years ago in the days of the gold standard, when every currency was pegged to gold and then pegged to each other by gold. Now every currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar and pegged to each other by the U.S. dollar. Precisely the same stagnation, the same strait-jacket has been created in the international monetary system by this arrangement as was the case when we had the gold standard across the world. It is time the Prime Minister, instead of saying "Heavens, no", said "Heavens, yes; I am going to start thinking about this problem." It is time this government took the initiative in international monetary arrangements of one sort or another to open up the thinking of the bankers and some of the businessmen toward considering a floating exchange rate system rather than a pegged one.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on the statement of the hon. Minister of Finance and say at the start that I cannot understand why it is that when there are such monetary crises just about everywhere in the world-we have seen many of them in the last few months and even in the last few years-the Canadian government, in co-operation with the other governments, does not appoint a royal commission of inquiry to look into the situation and report after a few months or even a few years to solve the problems which are submitted to it. That is what happens when there are internal problems, but when human beings are to be safeguarded, a situation improved, a commission of inquiry is appointed which reports after a few years, when it is realized that it is too late.
The Canadian government has just put at the disposal of the German mark and the French franc an amount of $100 million in order to save the currency that is in danger.
I feel the same steps should be taken to remedy the situation in Canada for, with regard to our internal affairs and the human being in Canada, especially in the field of unemployment, families, citizens, serious danger exists although there does not seem to be any corncern about what goes on here. I feel the same speed should be applied to solving our own problems and taking better care of human beings, instead of money and the monetary system.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
before the house deals with the estimates of the National Capital Commission for 1968-69, I would like to say a few words about the work of the commission for which I have been responsible since July 12, 1968.
Over the years, the house has been kept informed about the work of the commission through its annual reports and its capital investment programs tabled in the house. The work of the commission is based for the most part on the main recommendations of the


Greber report and is concerned with implementing the principles outlined to the house on June 28, 1948 when the National Capital Fund was set up. That fund was meant to supply the amounts needed to pay the cost of the undertakings approved by the governor in council to improve and develop the national capital. This is what the Prime Minister said at that time:
It also, and even more, seeks to anticipate the needs of Canada's capital in the future as we believe that future will shape our country. We desire, above all else, a capital worthy of the high place that Canada holds in the world today and of the Canada that is yet to be.
The national capital program designed by Mr. Jacques Greber, was tabled in the house in 1951. For the past 17 years, the government and the commission have amended and improved this plan. It was revised by a joint parliamentary committee which, in turn, recommended some changes. The committee report was tabled in the house on August 1, 1956. These changes, as well as the 12 years of experience in the meantime, have clearly demonstrated that the plan of a capital, like that of any other large city, has to be the continuing subject of criticism, studies and improvements.
In the meantime, the commission, by spending a great deal of time and money, had to acquire a large number of properties in order to implement the important recommendations of the plan. The period of time devoted to the acquisition of properties according to the recommendations of the plan is nearly over and the construction period is well under way. A new long term plan is being prepared in order to further improve and develop the national capital area. These new proposals will be introduced to the house in due time.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)

The commission's annual report for 1967-68, which has been tabled in the house, gives information of the commission's activities and expenditures for that year.
The estimates of the commission for 1968-69 amount to $24,500,000 for ordinary operations, interest on loans, improvements, and development within the national capital region, and $4,900,000 for loans to acquire property. These compare with $23,100,000 and $6,850,000 respectively in 1967-68. The actual expenditures for 1967-68 amounted to $21,600,000 gross. I have a detailed indication of the estimates,
November 25, 1968	COMMONS
and I hope this will be tabled so that hon. members will have it.

Serious consideration is now being given to the renovation of the centretown of Ottawa. Most parcels of land in the central area of the city, some belonging to the federal government, are ready to be re-developed. The commission had studies prepared on the economic prospects of the capital, with a view to establishing re-development plans to meet the needs and the prestige of the national capital.
That is one of the complex problems which holds the attention of the National Capital Commission, whose objectives are "to prepare plans for and assist in the development, conservation and improvement of the national capital region in order that the nature and character of the seat of the government of Canada may be in accordance with its national significance," Canada is a young country which, in all probability, will have a dynamic growth in the coming years. Ottawa, capital of Canada, is called to a brilliant future. Within the framework of its constitutional powers and thanks to its long experience in the field of town-planning, the commission plays a key role in the capital. Through its co-operation with the municipalities of the area, ensuring the wise use of federal properties and developing its own lands, the commission can make a valuable contribution to the expansion of the national capital. It will proceed with its town-planning work using tested techniques, allowing timely grants, encouraging general planning and the development of the lands and properties of the government, according to a long-term and flexible program.
Last year, in a speech which I delivered to the Chamber of Commerce in Hull, I noted the appreciable disproportion between the expenses made to improve the national capital-Ottawa-and those made for the improvement of the city of Hull. I wish to repeat today that the development plans of the national capital area should take into account not only the necessity of improving Hull-which is part of Ottawa on the economic as well as the social levels-but also the concern of the government to the effect that planning for the capital area in Quebec, especially in Hull, provides a just proportion of the over-all improvement proposed for the region. This planning must provide for the integration of the whole national capital area. It would be foolish to expect this undertaking to succeed while ignoring a vitally important
DEBATES	3137
Supply-National Capital Commission part of the area such as the city of Hull and the rest of the area which is located in Quebec.

My hon. friends will no doubt be conscious of the need to plan for a fair share of the development proposed for the national capital region to be made in Hull, Quebec, which for economic and social purposes is a part of the capital. It is my understanding that plans and proposals are being proposed to that end. The Promenade des Voyageurs, a parkway proposed for the Quebec side of the Ottawa river, from Hull to Deschenes, Quebec, a distance of approximately 5 miles, is an example of the improvements proposed for Hull. I cannot speak for my colleague, the Minister of Public Works, but I know that careful consideration is being given to the probable construction soon of federal government buildings in Hull. Also new bridges linking Hull closer to Ottawa are now being considered. All these proposals will contribute largely to the betterment of economic conditions in Hull and encourage the development of Hull, not as a poor suburb of Ottawa but on a comparable and competitive basis with Ottawa.
The commission, having put under way or completed the larger part of the recommendations contained in the Greber report, has reached an important crossroad in its planning for the region as a whole. Further, the creation of a new regional municipal authority in Ontario to absorb many of the responsibilities formerly borne by the city of Ottawa and other Ontario municipalities ought to pave the way for a much closer planning liaison between the regional council and the National Capital Commission. No doubt similar steps, if taken in the province of Quebec, would make the planning easier for that area of the national capital region. The government is deeply conscious of the need to promote to a greater extent the bilingual and bicultural aspect of the national capital region, so that it will be more truly representative of the founding peoples of this great country and, at the same time, be a living symbol of the unity and understanding which has prevailed since confederation.
I trust that these proposals will commend themselves to this committee.

The geographical area involved takes in parts of two great provinces or the two founding nations, so to speak, which have been put together to some extent in relation to these estimates. We must remember, in being slightly critical, that it has been five years since we have had the opportunity to discuss the estimates we are considering this afternoon. We must therefore take advantage of the opportunity to put forth sincerely constructive criticism in a manner which, if not in detail, will bring to the minister's attention the situation which exists.
If I may digress for a moment, we find that with greater regularity ministers are announcing government proposals outside this house, and I refer particularly to the minister's statements in respect of the proposed developments for Hull. Certainly we are in favour of these developments. The national capital area involves two cities, a number of municipalities and two provinces. In this regard we must consider this whole situation as one involving a language of its own. It seems to me it has become increasingly the policy of the government, in particular of certain ministers, to make statements outside the house.

Because a committee has not been set up for five years, we shall ask for and in fact insist upon such a committee being set up to study these problems. It should be a broad committee. I hope these remarks will be taken by the minister as constructive criticism. A committee of the house should be immediately set up to consider these estimates in great detail. It should consist of people interested in the development of our capital city. The provinces of Ontario and Quebec and the municipalities of Ottawa and Hull are not the only ones concerned with this question. People from all walks of life and all parts of this country are deeply concerned in the matter. This is why I suggest we should make sure that the committee is a very broad one.
As I have already pointed out, for five years nothing has been done in this respect, with the very laudable exception of the national gallery. I suppose here there have

been two mistakes. First, this is all that has been done in this long period of time and, second, there was the gross mistake of underestimating the cost of the national gallery. But I suppose things will work out in the end and I am not too critical of that mistake. During centennial year there were numerous functions on the lawns of parliament hill in our capital city. Here again I point out critically that in the last five years many things could have been done to culminate in centennial year. At least a committee could have been set up consisting of all the parties involved. One small matter that might have been considered by the committee is high-rise apartment buildings in Ottawa. This question has not even been properly considered. Why cannot these things be done? I suggest this is the place where these questions should be considered because we represent the whole of the country. In spite of the fact that some ministers and in fact the government itself would sometimes have us believe otherwise, this house is still the place where the people of Canada can speak.
The minister mentioned several things that have been done. I was glad to hear what he said about bridges. I was glad to hear the suggestion that a committee might study these matters. I cannot express my view too strongly that this whole question should be considered by a committee of the house. I do not refer to the one-man commission of Dr. Rowatt, I think it is, set up by the Ontario government. The federal government took part in it and took credit for it. However, I do not complain too much about that; it is probably a natural thing to do. The doctor has not yet reported, but the minister goes over to Hull and makes statements on these matters before the commission has reported. He also makes statements in the house before any committee has reported.
I suggest to you with all deference, Mr. Chairman, that statements of this kind should not be made before the commission and the committees report, because there are differences among the municipalities and, if I have to say it in so many words, there is a little distrust among them. Several prospective buildings in Hull have been mentioned. People in Eastview, Ottawa and the outlying municipalities have this distrust simply

because of a lack of knowledge and understanding of the matter. This emphasizes the fact that a committee should be set up to study these problems. Let everybody concerned have an understanding of what is involved.
The National Capital Commission and our capital city should really speak a language of their own in this country. We have the same problems. We have talked so much about them in this house in recent years, particularly last fall. These problems also concern other parts of the world. Neighbours living in the same community mistrust one another simply because of lack of understanding. If we understand one another, particularly our aims and views, I think there will no longer be any animosity. We find we have a common goal, we trust one another, and we reach that goal.
I thank the minister for his statement. I hope he will seriously consider the points that we in this party and all parties in the house have in mind. We are simply asking, and if we could we would demand it, that a broad committee be set up to undertake a detailed examination of these estimates. The minister must be aware that the commission has had a detailed report ready for two years, I understand, but no one has been able to listen to it. I think this is appalling. I refer to the commission whose estimates we are examining. The minister has said they are doing the planning; yet he goes to Hull and makes announcements there, as he does in this house, without reference to that report.
I ask that this committee be set up so we may have its ideas and recommendations. I believe this is only fair. I have tried to be sensible. I have been a little critical in order to bring forward these points. I hope the minister responsible for these matters will remember some of the points that have been raised and will take action to solve the problems that exist. I do not want to digress, Mr. Chairman, but we all have visitors from our constituencies from time to time. Constituents come here and say: Isn't the government in action wonderful? I sometimes wonder whether they are talking about one word or two words. It is time there was real action in this area on the part of the government.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to say a few words on the subject before us I am sure I feel very much like many other members of parliament in that we think of ourselves, at least in a way, as trustees of the public's money in our functions here regarding the

Here we are in the national capital of Canada surrounded by buildings, projects, landscaping and monuments to make it an even better capital for our country. Whether the Canadians who paid for it live in the eastern Arctic, in Frobisher Bay, away in the northeast or in my own southwestern area of Canada, in Surrey and White Rock city, they are all contributing, either in a small or in a major way, toward paying for what is being done here and for what is being planned for the national capital. Aside from these points I shall confine myself today to making a few criticisms regarding the situation in this area as I see it and our lack of perspective, planning and action. I should also like to reiterate the point which the previous speaker has made so well and which I and other members of our party have urged over the years. I refer to the wisdom of establishing a parliamentary committee on the national capital so that the members of this house will have a continuing and better understanding as well as an informed basis for their comments regarding what is being done with Canadian money in developing the national capital. I think that perhaps too high a priority has been given to the performing arts such as ballet. Let us seriously consider the fact that in Canada we have very little that relates us east to west; our thinking is apt to be directed toward the south. I find that in our culture, whether it is expressed in terms of the national capital or in terms of art or athletics, one part of our country, the mari-times, is entirely cut off from one of the greatest common denominators in our Canadian relationship, athletics. I am referring to the forthcoming national spectacle, the Grey cup game. If the parliament of Canada had had any say in regard to the spending of tax money to develop the national capital I wonder whether it might not have thought it better, instead of spending so many millions of dollars on building a structure here in Ottawa for the performing arts, perhaps to subsidize the city of Halifax so as to enable it to be represented in our national sports events. Perhaps this would be in the interest of the whole nation because I consider athletics to be a cultural activity, just as is opera or ballet, and one calculated to improve our national relationships. I think the house would have done something good for Canada if it had been able to give favourable consideration to such a suggestion.

During the 23 years I have been here I have said time and time again that one of the difficulties connected with improving this capital has been the lack of a close relationship between the provincial and federal governments. They were all always at loggerheads. In fact, they were not even at loggerheads because most of the time they did not even meet. Furthermore, there has always been a lack of liaison between the Department of Public Works and the city of Ottawa or the Prime Minister when he was in charge of the federal commission. We have had this trouble with zoning. There has never been a proper zoning plan of the city. There was little use in the National Capital Commission making plans when they were always running up against zoning which did not suit their plans. Even the departments within the government do not agree with each other. We have had clashes between the minister representing the National Capital Commission, the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of National Defence. At the moment there is a battle over zoning in the centre part of Ottawa. One builder desires to put up a very high building but the National Capital Commission opposes it. But, who will be the first tenant of that building if it is erected. The Department of Public Works. As long as there is no proper liaison between the province and the federal government or between the various departments of the government, plans cannot be made which will be useful.

We have made an error in pre-empting a stragetic location for the National Centre for the Performing Arts. I had visualized a beautiful, expansive view from parliament hill. But now we see a pile of stone that is supposed to typify or symbolize, as we were told in the committee, the great Canadian pre-Cambrian shield, as if that is the only thing representative of Canada. In this project there was a lack of imagination, a lack of vision. In fact, the main problem in the national capital area is the automobile which the majority of people use as a means of transportation in the cities. Most of the time, it is used strictly for personal prestige.

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry and Rural Development
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to go back over every problem put before the committee this afternoon. Let me merely point out that the powers of the National Capital Commission are extremely restricted, that is the only true powers it has are powers of expropriation. Besides those, the actual powers still belong to municipalities and the provincial government. So when the commission is blamed for not being perspicacious or for not doing certain things, in most cases, that is wrong, because the actual powers-even those of planning and development-belong to municipalities and to provinces, and not to the National Capital Commission.


In December 1967, the federal government, in co-operation with the Ontario and Quebec governments, established a special committee to study the problem of the national capital area. This committee has just reported to the Prime Minister of Canada and, through him, to the Ontario and Quebec premiers. This report has not yet been considered but it has been presented and we do hope that, in a short time-that is, within a few months-the government will have been able not only to formulate its own policy with regard to the National Capital area but, at the same time, to convince the provinces and the municipalities as to the best way to proceed in order to reach the objectives set forward in the legislation on the National Capital Commission.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I think that the most legitimate request formulated this afternoon was to the effect that a joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons, or a committee of the house only, be appointed to study more closely the estimates of the National Capital Commission and all its projects as well as, let us say, its procedure with regard to its objectives as set forth in the legislation.
I intend to set up that committee as soon as the government is ready to present an overall plan, on new structures or new objectives, which should be proposed to the National Capital Commission.
However, that may take months, Mr. Chairman, and I feel that the wisest thing to do would be for the committee to approve, this afternoon, the estimates as they stand and then wait until that committee is created. Personally, I feel it should be a joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate, so that the members who are interested can discuss at length, without any rush, the problem of the national capital which, as has already been mentioned, is not merely the problem of the people of Ottawa, or the people of Hull, but the problem of the whole Canadian people.
And so, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that this procedure should be followed. I suggest to those who have specific and well-founded problems, in most cases, that they wait, for I am convinced that they are not satisfied with the representations they made and that they intend to pursue the matter further. That opportunity will be given to them when a joint committee is set up which will have all the time required to look into the matter and report to the house.

speechtext:
That the standing committee on justice and legal affairs be empowered and directed to consider and report on the subject matter of electronic eavesdropping and to recommend legislative action which may be desirable and effective for its control.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I must confess that this motion was placed on the order paper in the hope that it would bring before the house more promptly than a private bill the subject of electronic eavesdropping. I first introduced a bill on this subject at the beginning of the twenty-seventh parliament. I have introduced a more refined bill in this parliament, but I recognize that neither my bill nor others dealing with the same subject which are on the order paper are adequate to cope with the very serious threat to freedom posed by electronic eavesdropping practised in this country.
I am glad to see that this danger has become better known within the last few months. I think there is now the prospect of action on the part of the government to recognize the invasion of privacy which electronic eavesdropping devices represent.
My own bill, Mr. Speaker, tries to raise and touch on most of the issues which have been considered by law, police and civil rights authorities in discussing electronic eavesdropping. It covers a somewhat wider field than proposals which deal with only wiretapping, a rather primitive form of electronic eavesdropping. I do not put forward the suggestions in my bill as the last word but rather as a basis for discussion, and I have submitted this motion in an effort to have the kind of public discussion which I feel is needed in order to develop adequate
Justice and Legal Affairs laws for the control of electronic eavesdropping. My own view is that electronic eavesdropping or wiretapping should be a criminal offence except when performed by police under strict statutory controls. My bill stresses the seriousness of this matter by providing for mandatory imprisonment of between one month and two years upon conviction of unauthorized use of any device for eavesdropping or interception of telephone and telegraph messages, and makes inadmissible in any trial or inquiry information obtained by such means where the use of such listening devices was not authorized in accordance with the statute.
I am encouraged by the fact that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) has indicated that he looks for legislation somewhat along these lines early in the coming year. I think it would be a mistake for the government to propose such legislation without having the benefit of public hearings and a great deal of technical data on this most complicated matter, as well as the opinions of interested individuals and groups in our country. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope that my motion will be accepted so that this most serious matter will receive the attention of the standing committee on justice and legal affairs in wide-ranging public hearings, and that legislative action will then be recommended by that committee for consideration by the government and by this house.
I do not see how any member of the house could fail to recognize the serious risk to our freedoms which wiretapping and electronic eavesdropping now constitute. I hope that all hon. members will support this effort to bring the practices in this field out into the open, to learn the extent of the problem, and to develop means of coping with it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to support the motion which is before the house because it seems to me this is a subject which requires a great deal more detailed consideration than it has been possible for it to receive up to this time. I think one of the main reasons for this situation is that traditionally the right of privacy has not been firmly established as one of those rights of the subject which have come down to us through the ages. It is a developing right, a modern right perhaps, as contrasted with some of those which we have had through centuries of English history.
The traditional political freedoms such as the freedom of the press, freedom of speech, freedom of religion, freedom of assembly and association, are those which are considered to be necessary for the continuance of our democratic system; they are those which are basic to the political process of this country. Freedom of speech is so directly related to this concept as to require no comment at all. The freedom of assembly, and even that of association, are also, I think, so directly related to the question of maintaining our democratic political system as to require no comment.
But the right of privacy does not have such an intrinsic place in terms of the political process; though I venture to say that many people in this country, if put to the test, if questioned whether they thought the right of privacy was an existing and important right, would perhaps contend that it is the most important right of all. It would seem to them, perhaps, to be more closely related to very fundamental matters such as the freedom of conscience and the freedom of religion.
This whole area has perhaps not been as firmly established in our jurisprudence and history as the more public rights. If we are ever to establish this right more firmly, to consider it not just in its context of wire tapping but also in the other manifestations which it may have in modern life, I think we will have to devote a great deal more study to this matter. This is now being done, of course, in other jurisdictions. In the United States a great deal of attention has recently been devoted to the question of the right of privacy, but it is not a right which in this country has been the subject of such great attention.

may be. That is a political question, and I hope something can be done about it.
I should like to remind those who suggest the introduction of compulsory measures that on May day, 1933, Hitler declared a national holiday, officially called the day of national labour. But on the following day trade union offices were occupied, union funds were confiscated, the unions were dissolved and their leaders arrested. Hitler brought in a law providing for the abolition of collective bargaining, and he said that henceforth labour disputes would be determined by trustees. Have we not all heard the term "labour trustee" recently? Hitler then went further and said that the decision of the trustees was to be legally binding. The law outlawed strikes. During the three years I have been in parliament I have learned of many sad cases involving men in their forties and fifties. These were cases of competent experienced men who had much to offer. They wanted to work. Many of them still had young families, but for many reasons they were unable to find employment. As a member of parliament I have endeavoured to help these men. I have spoken to personnel managers whom I know. I have tried to direct them to government jobs. In most cases, however, there seems to be some bar to the employment of men in these age categories.
If this is a serious problem today I maintain it will become much more serious unless some action is taken very shortly because, as many people have pointed out in this era of technological change and automation, many men will change their trade or employment during their lifetime, not once but two or three times. Hon. members who have spoken on the estimates so far have pointed out that men in their thirties, forties and fifties have been out of work after having been employed for many years. In these cases it is necessary for them quite often to develop new skills and look for a new type of work.
In the last few years the manpower retraining and relocation program has been introduced. This is a very good program under which we try to train men so that they will learn new skills, in order that they may fit into other employment. However, I believe all this will be of no avail if we do not do something about the restrictions and bars there seem to be in respect of employment for men in these age categories. The men who are faced with these problems are not only the blue collar workers; they are also the white collar workers, and professional people in all categories, some of whom have held very good positions for 20 or 30 years. Some of the cases I have known have involved men who have had the misfortune of being in hospital for a year or two because of serious illness. Then when they returned to the employment market they could not find anything.
It has been suggested that the solution to this problem might be through an amendment

to the Fair Employment Practices Act by adding discrimination in respect of age to the present categories of discrimination which are mentioned in that act.
